newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. elects judges for Yugoslav war crimes tribunal.
newsitem.headline: U.N. elects judges for Yugoslav war crimes tribunal.

text.p: The General Assembly elected on Tuesday nine of the 11 judges who will serve four-year terms on the U.N. war crimes tribunal for the former Yugoslavia, beginning on November 17.
Two other judges remain to be elected.
The tribunal, based at The Hague, was established by the Security Council in 1993. The terms of its original 11 judges expire in November.
The Security Council last month nominated 19 candidates. The final choice was up to the Assembly, where an absolute majority of 94 votes was needed to win election.
The following jurists were elected by the Assembly in the first round of ballotting:

Antonio Cassese of Italy, the court's current president (146 votes); Richard May of Britain (129); Mohamed Shahabuddeen of Guyana (127); Wang Tieya of China (123); Claude Jorda of France (119); Gabrielle Kirk McDonald of the United States (118); Fouad Abdel-Moneim Riad of Egypt (118); Lal Chand Vohrah of Malaysia (113); and Rafael Nieto Navia of Colombia (96).
Five of those elected are currently serving on the court -- Cassese, Jorda, McDonald, Riad and Vohrah.
The tribunal is the first international body for the prosecution of war crimes since the Nuremberg and Tokyo trials held in the aftermath of the Second World War.
It has so far indicted 75 suspects -- 54 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems.

The first full-length trial ended earlier this month when Dusan "Dusko" Tadic, a Bosnian Serb police reservist, was found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity for his part in a Serb "ethnic cleansing" campaign against Bosnian Moslems in 1992. He awaits sentencing. The tribunal cannot impose death sentences.
A Bosnian Croat, Drazen Erdemovic, has been sentenced to 10 years in jail after confessing to killing unarmed Moslems at Srebrenica in 1995.
Six more men are in custody in the tribunal's detention centre awaiting trial.
The two most prominent indicted suspects, who are both at large, are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander General Ratko Mladic.
